title: Knowledge Check 3: Lessons 11-15
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 11-15 of the hermes-consultant series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Which task is ready to become a recurring scheduled job?
options: One that worked once but needed your judgment at several points
One you are confident will behave the same way next week without testing
One that produced a reliable result when you ran it by hand
One that is barely stitched together but saves time if it works
questions.explanation: You automate a win that already works reliably by hand; scheduling something unproven just automates a failure on a fixed timetable.

questions.question: Why must a scheduled job's instructions be self-contained?
options: Because every run starts in a fresh session that inherits none of your context
Because the scheduler rejects a prompt that names more than one external system
Because the model forgets the names of its tools between separate executions of a job
Because unattended runs are forbidden from calling any tool that needs a credential
questions.explanation: A scheduled run is a fresh session with none of your memory, so the prompt must carry the target, the action, and the output shape on its own.

questions.question: A scheduled job completed and produced its report, but no one received it. What is the correct reading?
options: The job succeeded, because a completed run always reaches its recipient
The failure is unrelated to the schedule and can be ignored
The report should be regenerated by hand and sent again
This is a delivery failure, which fails separately from the run itself
questions.explanation: Run failure and delivery failure are tracked separately, so a job whose output reaches nobody has not delivered anything even though it ran.

questions.question: What is the orchestrator's role in a portfolio of agent work?
options: To personally finish the most important card so that it is certain to ship correctly
To decompose the goal, assign each card, and step back from doing the work
To watch every worker closely and correct its output while the work is produced
To reassign each card to a new worker at every stage to build in redundancy
questions.explanation: An orchestrator scales by turning a goal into cards, assigning each to the right worker, and stepping back rather than becoming the bottleneck.

questions.question: Where should a card's acceptance criteria live, and why?
options: In a shared document that the worker is instructed to open before it begins the task
In the orchestrator's private memory, which the worker can query whenever it needs to
In the assignee's prior handoffs from similar tasks it has completed before
On the card itself, because the worker reads only the card and its own thread
questions.explanation: The worker reads only the card and its thread, so the definition of done must sit on the card in verifiable terms or no one can check it.

questions.question: What is required for a worker to finish a task correctly?
options: A terminal call that completes with proof or blocks with a clear reason
Stopping work once the main changes have already been written to disk and saved
Marking the task done as soon as the changes appear to be complete and correct
Leaving a short written summary and letting the dispatcher decide the final status
questions.explanation: A portfolio runs unattended, so the worker must close with a terminal call that proves completion or states a blocker; merely stopping can pass a start off as done.

questions.question: What makes a piece of data a secret?
options: Its length and the mix of unusual characters that appear inside it
Whether it is stored inside a file that ends in the env extension
The fact that the client specifically asked you to keep the value private
The access it unlocks, no matter how short or unremarkable it looks
questions.explanation: A secret is defined by the access it unlocks, not by its appearance, so a short token that reaches customer records is treated with full care.

questions.question: Why must least privilege be enforced by guardrails rather than by the agent behaving carefully?
options: Because a careful agent runs faster than one that has to ask permission for each action
Because a guardrail refuses on its own when care fails, as with a hostile input
Because guardrails make the agent's own output more accurate and more complete
Because a client cannot observe what the agent does without enforced limits in place
questions.explanation: Guardrails are mechanisms that refuse; they hold when the agent is careless or a hostile input steers it, which is exactly when carefulness fails.

questions.question: What is the correct default for dangerous commands in unattended scheduled work?
options: Approve them automatically so that the recurring job never stalls partway through
Let the agent decide for itself whether each individual command is safe to run
Deny them, so the job must find a safe path or fail in a way that is visible
Approve them only after the job has already run successfully several times
questions.explanation: Unattended work defaults to denying dangerous commands, because a failure you can see is safer than a destructive command that no one approved.

questions.question: An agent reports that it updated a record. What does this statement represent?
options: A claim, which is not proof until the record itself is read back and checked
A verified result, because the agent says it completed the task it described
A repeatable gate, because the same update could be applied again later on
A tool trace, because the agent has named the specific action it performed
questions.explanation: What the agent says is a claim, and only reading the result back in the system turns that claim into evidence.

questions.question: A command is run through a terminal tool. Which evidence tells you whether it actually succeeded?
options: The sentence the agent writes summarizing what the command did
The agent stating that the command completed without any errors
The command's actual output and its exit code
The length of time the command took to finish running
questions.explanation: The tool's real output and exit code are the evidence; a summary sentence about the command is not proof that it ran correctly.

questions.question: Watching a tool fire proves the agent tried. What does it take to prove the result is correct?
options: A second run that produces output of roughly the same length as the original run did
Reading the result back in the system and comparing it against the source
An exit code of zero from the command that produced the reported result
A clean diff showing that the intended file on disk was modified as planned
questions.explanation: Effort is not correctness, so the result is verified in the system against the source the way the client's team would use it.

questions.question: What is the difference between a plan and an artifact?
options: A plan is the deliverable the client pays for, and an artifact is optional supporting detail
A plan runs against the live system, and an artifact describes what the plan will do
A plan describes work someone intends to do, and an artifact is the work itself
A plan is verified by a checklist, and an artifact is verified by a human reviewer
questions.explanation: Clients pay for the working result they can run or verify, while a description of intended work is only a plan dressed up as delivery.

questions.question: An agent cannot reach the client's database. What is the correct way to finish?
options: Report that the database was unreachable, why, and what would unblock it
Report a plausible record count so that the deliverable still looks complete to the client
Mark the task as done and quietly note the missing data in a later status update
Reuse the numbers from the last available run and present them as the current result
questions.explanation: Fabrication is invisible and poisonous, so stating the real blocker with its reason and what would unblock it preserves both the truth and the relationship.

questions.question: Which statement reflects the finishing discipline?
options: Saying it should work is an acceptable status whenever the design itself looks sound
A run that completed is the same thing as a verified and working final result
Capturing what the work taught you is an optional step once the task is delivered
A claim is finished only when verified, and the reusable part is captured
questions.explanation: Verification is the finish line, and capturing the reusable part lets the next piece of work start further along than the last one did.
